title: Problem Overview
content:
**Erdős Problem #1126: Almost Additive Functions**

If f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y) for almost all pairs (x,y), can f be 'repaired' to satisfy the equation for ALL pairs?

**Answer: YES** — proved by de Bruijn (1966) and Jurkat (1965) independently.

The repaired function g agrees with f almost everywhere and is unique among additive functions.
mathContext: Connects Cauchy's functional equation with measure theory.

title: Cauchy's Functional Equation
content:
**IsAdditive f:** f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y) for all x,y ∈ ℝ.

The simplest examples are f(x) = cx for any constant c. If f is also continuous, then f(x) = cx is the only possibility (Cauchy's classical result). Without continuity, wild solutions exist via the Axiom of Choice.

title: Almost Additive Functions
content:
**IsAlmostAdditive f:** f(x+y) = f(x) + f(y) for almost all pairs (x,y) ∈ ℝ².

'Almost all' means the equation fails only on a null set in ℝ² (Lebesgue measure zero). Also defines ae_holds (a.e. for single variable), ae_pairs (a.e. for pairs), and ae_eq (equal a.e.).

title: de Bruijn-Jurkat Theorem
content:
**de_bruijn_jurkat_theorem:** If f is almost additive, there exists a truly additive g with f = g almost everywhere.

The 'defects' in almost-additivity can always be repaired by changing f on a null set! This is the main result of Erdős Problem #1126.

title: Uniqueness of Correction
content:
**additive_ae_unique:** If g₁ and g₂ are both additive and equal a.e., then g₁ = g₂ everywhere.

This follows from the key lemma: an additive function that is zero a.e. must be identically zero. So the repair g in the main theorem is unique.

title: Wild Functions and Regularity
content:
**wild_additive_exist:** Discontinuous additive functions exist (using AC).

**measurable_additive_is_linear:** If f is additive and Lebesgue measurable, then f(x) = cx.

Wild additive functions are necessarily non-measurable. This context shows why the almost-additivity question is subtle.

title: Summary Theorem
content:
**erdos_1126_summary:** Combines the main theorem (de Bruijn-Jurkat) with uniqueness into a single result.

Proved directly from the axiomatized results.

**SOLVED** by de Bruijn (1966) and Jurkat (1965).
